title: The Art of War
author: Sun Tzu
openingText: The words of Sun the Master: To all nations War is a great matter. Upon the army death or life depend: it is the means of the existence or destruction of the State. Therefore it must be diligently studied. Now, in war, besides stratagem and the situation, there are five indispensable matters. The first is called The Way; the second, Heaven; the third, Earth; the fourth, the Leader; the fifth, Law.
about:
The Art of War is a short Chinese treatise on military strategy, traditionally attributed to the general Sun Tzu, who is said to have served the king of Wu in the late 6th or early 5th century BCE. It is arranged in thirteen brief chapters, each on one part of warfare: the preliminary reckoning, the operations of war, the attack by stratagem, the order of battle, the spirit of the troops, emptiness and strength, battle tactics, the nine changes, the movement of troops, ground, the nine grounds, assault by fire, and the employment of spies. The chapters are short and the sentences terse. The argument is that real victory comes from understanding rather than force, from preparation rather than boldness, and from knowing the enemy better than he knows himself.

The text was preserved in Chinese military and political tradition for some two and a half thousand years and reached European readers through a French translation in 1772. It has been studied by Napoleon, Mao Zedong and Ho Chi Minh, and by military academies in China and the United States. A bamboo-slip copy excavated from a Han-dynasty tomb in 1972 confirmed the basic shape of the received text. The English text in Tinct is the 1908 translation by Captain E. F. Calthrop, The Book of War, with a Tinct modern English rendering alongside it.

The book is one of the most concentrated treatments of conflict in any tradition. Its central insight is that a battle, when it happens, marks a failure of strategy: the best commander wins through manoeuvre, pretence, and the management of supply and morale before any troops meet. It is also a study of self-knowledge, patience and the price of misjudgement. People who never expected to fight a war have read it for centuries, because what it says about preparation, intelligence and timing applies wherever serious decisions are made.

angleCards.title: Winning without fighting.
angleCards.text: Sun Tzu's central claim is that the supreme art is to subdue the enemy without fighting. I want to follow that principle through all thirteen chapters and understand what it demands of a commander — in preparation, intelligence and patience.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Art of War as a philosophy of minimum force — the idea that the best general wins without fighting, and what that principle actually means in practice.

angleCards.title: War as a psychological contest.
angleCards.text: Sun Tzu is less interested in weapons than in morale, deception, and information. I want to track how consistently he treats the outcome of battles as already decided by psychological conditions — and whether that holds up against history.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Art of War as an argument that all conflict is psychological before it is physical — that what happens in the minds of commanders and troops determines the outcome before anyone draws a weapon.

angleCards.title: Beyond the battlefield.
angleCards.text: The book has been applied to business strategy, sports, and personal decision-making for decades. I want to read it with those applications in mind — not to flatten the military context, but to find where the principles genuinely generalise and where the analogy breaks.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to apply the principles outside their military context — to negotiation, business, or personal decisions — and test which ones actually translate.

angleCards.title: Self-knowledge as strategy.
angleCards.text: "He who knows both sides has nothing to fear in a hundred fights." I want to take that claim seriously — what does it mean to truly know yourself in a conflict, and what does Sun Tzu say it requires?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand what Sun Tzu means by knowing both the enemy and oneself — what it actually takes to achieve that, and why he treats it as the foundation of everything else.

cast.name: Sun Tzu
cast.description: Chinese general and military theorist, traditionally identified with Sun Wu, who served the southern state of Wu against the larger northern state of Chu in the late 6th century BCE. Whether the text is the work of one historical man or a tradition compiled under his name is still debated. The voice in the book is unified: calm, exact, pitched at a king who must commit a state to war and at the general who must execute it without losing the army or the country.

cast.name: The General
cast.description: A composite figure described throughout the text — calm, adaptable, informed, holding the whole of a campaign in mind without showing strain. He is an instrument of precision rather than a heroic personality. He must be ready to disobey his lord when the situation demands it, to refuse battle when it is offered, and to retreat without loss of face. Sun Tzu names five dangerous faults in a general: blind impetuosity, over-cautiousness, quick temper, a too rigid propriety, and over-regard for the troops.

cast.name: The Sovereign
cast.description: The political authority who commits the state to war and must then keep his hands off its conduct. Sun Tzu is explicit. A prince who orders advances or retreats he does not understand, who governs the army as he governs the state, or who fixes its dispositions without knowing its situation leaves his soldiers perplexed and distrustful, and neighbouring princes take advantage. Victory can be foretold when an able general is not interfered with by his prince.

cast.name: The Enemy
cast.description: Not to be hated, not to be underestimated, not to be made into a moral category. The enemy is a system to be read: their morale, their supply lines, their commanders' temperament, the quarrels in their court, the season and the terrain in which they must fight. Sun Tzu treats contempt as a strategic liability. The general who knows the enemy as well as he knows his own forces fights from a position the enemy cannot match. The general who does not is gambling.

cast.name: The Terrain
cast.description: Sun Tzu gives three of his thirteen chapters largely to ground. He sorts it into six kinds: open ground, broken ground, suspended ground, defiles, precipices and far countries. He also names nine grounds by the situation they create: distracting, disturbing, ground of contention, intersecting, path-ridden, deeply-involved, difficult, enclosed and death ground. Ground is not passive scenery. It decides what is possible, and a general who has not studied the ground he will fight on has lost before the engagement begins.

cast.name: The Spy
cast.description: The subject of the final chapter, and Sun Tzu's argument suggests it could as well have come first. He names five kinds — village spies, inner spies (enemy officials in one's pay), converted spies (the enemy's own spies turned), death spies (sent to carry false reports), and living spies, who return to report. Without them, every other principle in the book rests on guesswork. With them, the general knows the enemy's situation before he moves.

acclaim.quote: We must not belittle the saying in the book of Sun Wu Tzu, the great military expert of ancient China
acclaim.context: On Protracted War, 1938, introducing Sun Tzu's saying on knowing the enemy and knowing oneself

whyItMatters.title: Winning Without Fighting
whyItMatters.body: The book argues that the highest form of victory is the one in which no battle is fought. Sun Tzu prefers courses that make fighting unnecessary — understanding the opponent so well that he yields, holding ground that makes attack pointless, keeping the enemy from uniting his forces before he reaches the field. In Calthrop's translation, "the supreme art is to subdue the enemy without fighting." Below that comes outwitting the enemy by stratagem, then preventing his forces from joining, then engaging his army, and last and worst, besieging his citadel. The principle has shaped Chinese military thinking for some twenty-five centuries and Western thinking since the first French translation. It now appears in business strategy courses, negotiation training and discussions of deterrence.

whyItMatters.title: Knowing the Self and the Enemy
whyItMatters.body: Sun Tzu's best-known formula — he who knows both sides has nothing to fear in a hundred fights; he who knows only his own side wins once and loses the next time; he who knows neither is invariably defeated — sums up the book's method. Strategy is first of all a discipline of knowledge. Most defeats, on Sun Tzu's account, come from not knowing one's own position or the enemy's. The formula is simple, but what it asks is severe. Knowing oneself means knowing not only one's forces but one's temperament — whether one leans toward rashness or caution, and whether anger or pride is the likelier failing. Commanders, executives and competitors still fall short of it in much the way Sun Tzu expected.

whyItMatters.title: A Manual That Survived Empires
whyItMatters.body: The book has been read in China since the Warring States period — through the Han, the Tang, the Song, the Mongol conquest, the Ming, the Qing, the Republic and the People's Republic. It has lasted because what it says about conflict is recognisable in every age of organised human effort. Generals across the centuries have tested it against real war and kept returning to it. Versions of it are read at military academies in both China and the United States. The whole text is shorter than a single chapter of most modern strategy books, and it has outlasted nearly all of them. Sun Tzu reduces each principle to its working core, and that brevity is part of what so many readers have found worth keeping.
